name: The Hall of Forking Ways
goal: Direct a program down different paths using conditions, and predict which path runs.

description.what: How a program asks a yes-or-no question about a value and then does something different depending on the answer.
description.why: Every program that is worth writing behaves differently in different situations - a price that depends on age, a message that depends on whether anything was found - and a condition is the only way to say so.
description.enables: Write a program that chooses between several outcomes, combine several questions into one, and say in advance which branch a given value will take.
description.assumes: You can write and run a small program, store a value under a name, and work out the value and type of an expression by hand.
description.assessed: You will predict what branching programs print, repair ones that branch wrongly, and write programs that pick their own path from a stated set of rules.

sections.title: A condition is an expression that answers yes or no
sections.body:
Python has a type whose values are answers to questions. It is called **bool**, and it has exactly two values, written `True` and `False` - capital letter, no quotation marks. `True` is not the same thing as the piece of text `"True"`, and mixing the two up is the first mistake almost everybody makes.

You produce a bool by **comparing** two values. There are six comparison operators: `==` is equal to, `!=` is not equal to, `<` less than, `>` greater than, `<=` less than or equal to, `>=` greater than or equal to. Note the doubled `==`. A single `=` gives a name to a value, which is a completely different act, and Python will refuse the program rather than guess which you meant.

The important idea is that a comparison is an ordinary expression, exactly like `3 + 4`. It is worked out down to a single value before anything else happens to it, so you may print it, store it under a name, or hand it to the `if` you will meet in the next section. Python also lets you chain comparisons: `1 < x < 10` means what it looks like it means, and is worked out as both halves being true at once.

One warning that costs people real hours. Numbers with a decimal point are stored as approximations, so `0.1 + 0.2` is very slightly not `0.3` and `==` reports `False`. Comparing two such numbers for exact equality is nearly always the wrong test; ask instead whether the gap between them is small enough to ignore.
sections.code:
temperature = 4
freezing = temperature < 0
print(freezing)
print(temperature == 4)
print(0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3)
print(1 < temperature < 10)

annotations.text: The comparison is worked out first and produces a bool; `freezing` now refers to `False` in the same way a name could refer to `7` or to a piece of text. Nothing here is a question waiting to be asked later - it is an answer, already computed.

This prints `False`, and the program is not wrong. `0.1 + 0.2` is stored as 0.30000000000000004, so exact equality genuinely fails. This is the single commonest surprise with decimal numbers in every language, not a quirk of Python.

A chained comparison. Python reads it as `1 < temperature` and `temperature < 10` both holding, which is the mathematical reading. Most languages do not allow this and would give you nonsense instead.

checkpoint.explain: `x != 5` asks whether they differ, and they do not, so it is `False`. `x >= 5` succeeds on the equal case, which is exactly the difference between `>` and `>=` - and the boundary where most off-by-one faults live.

sections.title: if, elif, else - and the indentation that makes them real
sections.body:
`if` takes a condition and a block of statements indented beneath it, and runs that block only when the condition is `True`. `else` takes a block that runs when it was `False`. `elif` - short for "else if" - lets you test a further condition only when every condition above it has already failed.

A chain runs **at most one** branch. Python tests the conditions from the top and stops dead at the first one that is `True`, never looking at the rest. That is why `elif` is not the same as writing a second `if`: two separate `if` statements are two independent decisions and both blocks can run, while an `if`/`elif` chain is one decision with several possible outcomes. If your branches overlap, the order you write them in is part of the logic.

Indentation is not tidiness in Python; it is the syntax that says what belongs to the branch. Four spaces is the convention. A line indented under the `if` runs only when the condition holds, and the same line moved back out to the left runs every time. Changing the indentation of a line changes the meaning of the program, silently and completely.

From here on, some exercises ask you for a **function**: a named recipe, written `def price(age):`, that is handed a value - here called `age` - and uses `return` to hand an answer back to whoever asked. Floor 7 teaches functions properly. For now, read `def` as "here is a recipe with a name", and `return` as "this is the answer, stop here".

annotations.text: `age < 18` is only ever tested when `age < 5` has already failed, so this branch quietly means "between 5 and 17". Written as a separate `if`, it would also catch a 3-year-old and the order of the branches would stop protecting you.

`else` carries no condition because it cannot fail: it is everything the branches above did not catch. Every value of `age` therefore reaches exactly one `return`, which is what makes this recipe total rather than sometimes silent.
18 is not less than 18, so both conditions fail and the `else` runs. Boundary values like this one are where branching code is worth testing first, not last.

checkpoint.prompt: Write `sign_word(n)`. It returns the text `"positive"` when `n` is greater than zero, `"negative"` when `n` is less than zero, and `"zero"` when it is neither.
checkpoint.hint: Three outcomes need three branches. The last one needs no condition at all, because anything that is neither above nor below zero is zero.
checkpoint.explain: Zero is the case people forget, because `> 0` and `< 0` between them look as though they cover the number line and they do not. Leaving it out does not raise an error - the recipe simply hands back nothing at all for zero, which is a far harder fault to notice.

sections.title: and, or, not - and the half Python never reads
sections.body:
Three words combine conditions. `a and b` is `True` only when both are; `a or b` is `True` when at least one is; `not a` flips the answer over. They bind with different strengths - `not` tightest, then `and`, then `or` - so `not x and y` means `(not x) and y`. When a combination takes more than a moment to read, put brackets in and stop relying on the rule.

The part worth remembering is that these two operators are lazy, which is called **short-circuit** evaluation. `and` works out the left side first, and if it is `False` the whole thing is already `False`, so the right side is never worked out at all. `or` does the mirror image: a `True` on the left ends it. This is not an optimisation you can ignore - it is a tool. Putting the cheap or protective test on the left lets it guard the dangerous one on the right, which is how `count != 0 and total / count > 5` avoids dividing by zero.

You can also put an `if` inside another `if`, which is called **nesting**, and the indentation shows what sits inside what. When the outer branch contains nothing but the inner `if`, nesting and `and` say exactly the same thing, and the flat version with `and` is easier to read. Nest when the outer branch has its own work to do, or its own `else` for the case where the outer test fails - because a flat `and` cannot tell you which half failed.
sections.code:
count = 0
total = 0
if count != 0 and total / count > 5:
    print("high average")
else:
    print("no average to report")

is_member = True
age = 70
print(age < 12 or age >= 65)
print(not is_member)

annotations.text: `count != 0` is `False`, so Python never works out the division and the program does not crash. Swap the two halves round and the same program dies with a ZeroDivisionError - the order of an `and` can be the difference between working and failing.
An `or` where both halves are ordinary comparisons: 70 is not under 12, but it is 65 or over, so one `True` is enough and the whole expression is `True`.
`not` takes the bool on its right and returns the other one. It does not modify `is_member`; like every operator so far it produces a new value and leaves its input alone.

checkpoint.prompt: Write `can_vote(age, is_citizen)`. It returns `True` when the person is 18 or older **and** `is_citizen` is `True`, and `False` otherwise. `is_citizen` is already a bool.
checkpoint.solution:
def can_vote(age, is_citizen):
    return age >= 18 and is_citizen
checkpoint.hint: You do not need an `if` at all. The combined condition is already the answer, so it can be handed back directly.
checkpoint.explain: Writing `if age >= 18 and is_citizen: return True else: return False` works, but it takes a bool, tests it, and then builds the same bool again. When the answer you want is the condition itself, hand the condition back - and note that `is_citizen == True` is the same redundancy in miniature.

sections.title: Truthiness, and what an empty thing means
sections.body:
`if` does not insist on a bool. It accepts any value at all and applies a fixed rule to decide whether that value counts as a yes. Values that count as no are called **falsy**, and the list is short: `False`, the number `0` (and `0.0`), empty text `""`, and `None` - which is Python's word for the deliberate absence of any value. Every other value is **truthy**, including negative numbers, and including the piece of text `"0"`, which is not empty and therefore counts as a yes.

This is convenient. `if name:` reads as "if there is a name" and covers the empty case without a comparison. Groups of values that arrive on later floors follow exactly the same rule: an empty one is falsy, a non-empty one is truthy.

It is also a trap, and it is worth naming precisely. Truthiness collapses several very different situations into one answer. A stock count of `0` means sold out; a stock count of `None` means nobody has counted yet. Both are falsy, so `if count:` treats them identically and the difference you cared about disappears without any error being raised.

The rule of thumb: when the falsy values are genuinely all the same to you, lean on truthiness. When zero is a real, meaningful value, test for what you actually mean - `count is None` for absent, `count == 0` for sold out. `is None` is the standard way to test for `None`, and it is worth reading as one word.

annotations.text: `name` is not a bool, and Python does not complain. Empty text is falsy, so the `else` runs. This is the idiom for "did I actually get anything?" and it is why an empty name never reaches the greeting.

`bool(value)` reports the very answer `if` would use, which makes it the way to check your understanding of any value. `"0"` is text one character long, so it is truthy - the digit inside it is not consulted.

This chain distinguishes the two falsy cases that mattered, in the order that matters: absent first, then zero. Written as `if not count:` both would land in the same branch and the program would say the wrong thing without ever failing.

checkpoint.prompt: Write `greeting(name)`. When `name` is a non-empty piece of text it returns `"Hello, "` followed by the name. When `name` is empty text it returns `"Hello, stranger"`.
checkpoint.hint: Empty text is falsy, so the name itself can be the condition - no comparison with `""` is needed, though one would work.
checkpoint.explain: `if name != "":` is correct here and reads fine, but it only covers empty text, while `if name:` also catches `None` if a missing name ever arrives that way. That breadth is the attraction of truthiness, and on the next floor of your own code it will also be the risk.

guided-practice.explain: The first line is the decimal-approximation trap: the sum is 0.30000000000000004. The third line catches people because `not` looks as though it grabs the `5`; it does not - comparison binds tighter than `not`, so Python works out `5 > 3` first and then flips the `True` it produced.

Two separate `if` statements are two separate decisions, so both run for a value that satisfies both. The `elif` version is one decision, and it stops at the first success - which is why swapping `elif` for a second `if` is never a cosmetic edit.

guided-practice.prompt: Fill the blanks. The first message should appear only when there is something to average and that average is above 5. The second should appear when either number is zero.
guided-practice.explain: The first blank must be `and` for two reasons at once: both parts have to hold, and the left part has to protect the division on the right from a zero. The second blank is `or` because either zero on its own is enough to leave you with nothing worth reporting.

guided-practice.prompt: `ticket_price(age)` should charge 0 for anyone under 5, 5 for anyone under 18, 5 for anyone 65 or over, and 10 for everybody else. It is right for children and pensioners but hands back nothing at all for a 30-year-old. Repair it.
guided-practice.hint: Look at what the last line belongs to. Which values of `age` can ever reach it where it currently sits?
guided-practice.explain: `return 10` is indented under the `age >= 65` branch, so it sits after a `return` that has already left - it can never run, and a 30-year-old falls off the end of the recipe and gets nothing. Python raises no error, because the indentation is legal; it simply describes a different program from the one intended. That is what "indentation is syntax" costs when you get it wrong.

guided-practice.prompt: Write `describe_stock(count)`. `count` is `None` when nobody has counted the shelf yet, and otherwise a whole number. Return `"unknown"` for `None`, `"out of stock"` for 0, and `"in stock"` for anything higher.
guided-practice.hint: Test for the absent case first and by name, then for zero, then let everything else fall through.
guided-practice.explain: The tempting first attempt is `if not count: return "unknown"`, which passes the `None` test and then quietly mislabels a sold-out shelf as uncounted. Both values are falsy, so truthiness cannot separate them; only `is None` and `== 0` can, and the order matters because `None == 0` is `False` but `None` would still be caught by any truthiness test placed first.

independent-practice.prompt: A clinic labels a body-mass index as follows: below 18.5 is `"under"`; from 18.5 up to but not including 25 is `"normal"`; from 25 up to but not including 30 is `"over"`; 30 and above is `"obese"`. Write `bmi_category(bmi)` returning the right label.
independent-practice.explain: Every boundary here belongs to the band above it, so each test is a strict `<` and the value 25 lands in `"over"`. Testing from the bottom upwards means each later condition can assume the earlier ones failed, which is why none of them needs a lower bound written out.

independent-practice.prompt: A shop charges 5 to ship an order, plus 3 more when it weighs more than 10 kg. Members ship free, but only for orders of 2 kg or less; a heavier member order is charged like anyone else's. Write `shipping_cost(weight, is_member)` returning the amount charged. `is_member` is a bool.
independent-practice.explain: The free case needs both facts to hold at once, and once it has been handled the rest of the recipe no longer has to think about membership at all. Charging 5 first and then adding 3 works equally well; what fails is treating membership as a discount applied everywhere, because a 12 kg member order pays full price.

independent-practice.prompt: A year in the Gregorian calendar is a leap year when it divides exactly by 4, except that a year dividing exactly by 100 is not, unless it also divides exactly by 400 - so 1996 and 2000 are leap years and 1900 is not. Write `is_leap_year(year)` returning `True` or `False`.
independent-practice.explain: The rule has an exception to an exception, so the surest way through it is to answer the most specific case first and let the general case fall to the bottom. Written as one combined expression it is also correct - `year % 4 == 0 and (year % 100 != 0 or year % 400 == 0)` - and the brackets there are not optional, because `and` binds tighter than `or` and dropping them changes the answer for 1900.

independent-practice.prompt: A profile page shows a person's nickname if they gave one, and their full name if they did not. A nickname that was never supplied arrives as `None`, and one that was submitted blank arrives as empty text; both mean "they did not give one". Write `display_name(nickname, full_name)` returning the text to show.
independent-practice.explain: Here the two empty cases genuinely mean the same thing, so collapsing them is the right call rather than a shortcut - this is precisely the situation truthiness exists for. Writing `if nickname is not None:` would pass three tests and show a blank name for the fourth, because empty text is not `None`.

independent-practice.prompt: Given three side lengths, report what triangle they make. Sides that are zero or negative, or where the two shorter sides do not add up to more than the longest, do not make a triangle at all and should give `"not a triangle"`. Otherwise return `"equilateral"` when all three match, `"isosceles"` when exactly two match, and `"scalene"` when none do. Write `classify_triangle(a, b, c)`.
independent-practice.explain: Validity has to be settled before shape, because 1, 2 and 3 would otherwise be reported as a perfectly good scalene triangle - the flat case where the sides lie in a straight line is exactly why the test is `<=` and not `<`. Ordering equilateral before isosceles matters too: all three equal also satisfies "two are equal", so the more specific test has to come first.

exam.prompt: In an `if` / `elif` / `elif` / `else` chain, three of the conditions happen to be `True`. How many branches run?
choices: One - the first true one, and the rest are never tested
All three true ones, in order
None; Python reports an ambiguous chain
exam.explain: A chain is one decision with several possible outcomes, so it stops at the first success. The tempting answer is "all three", which is what would happen with three separate `if` statements - and confusing the two is the reason overlapping branches have to be ordered from most specific to most general.

exam.prompt: Which of these values are falsy - that is, which would send an `if` to its `else`?
exam.explain: Falsy means `False`, `None`, zero and empty. The two distractors are the ones that catch people: `"0"` is a piece of text one character long, so it is not empty and counts as a yes, and -1 is truthy because the rule is about being zero, not about being positive.

`loud` announces itself whenever it is worked out, so counting the word `checked` counts the halves Python actually read. The first two conditions are settled by their left side alone and never touch `loud`; only the third has to look right, and even then its answer is `False`, so nothing follows it.

exam.code:
print(bool("0"))
print(bool(0.0))
if "False":
    print("text is truthy")
exam.explain: Text is judged on whether it is empty, never on what it says, so `"0"` and `"False"` are both yeses while the number `0.0` is a no. This is the exact fault behind text read from a keyboard or a file being treated as `True` when it plainly says `False`.

exam.prompt: A person may drive if they are 18 or over, or if they hold a permit. Fill the blanks so the warning prints exactly when they may not.
exam.explain: The permission is an `or`, and the warning is its opposite, so the whole permission goes in brackets and `not` is applied to the result. Without the brackets `not age >= 18 or has_permit` reads as `(not (age >= 18)) or has_permit`, which prints the warning for any adult holding a permit.

exam.prompt: Arrange these lines into a working recipe that returns `'gold'` for 90 and above, `'silver'` for 70 and above, and `'bronze'` for anything lower.
exam.explain: The higher threshold has to be tested first: with `score >= 70` at the top, a score of 95 satisfies it and never reaches the gold branch. The indentation carries the rest of the meaning - each `return` is indented one level deeper than the branch that owns it.

exam.prompt: Two bookings each run from a start hour to an end hour, and both ends count as occupied. Write `overlaps(a_start, a_end, b_start, b_end)` returning `True` when the two share at least one hour and `False` when they do not.
exam.starterCode:
def overlaps(a_start, a_end, b_start, b_end):
    return False
exam.solution:
def overlaps(a_start, a_end, b_start, b_end):
    return a_start <= b_end and b_start <= a_end
exam.explain: It is far easier to say when two ranges miss each other - one finishes before the other starts - and to deny it, than to enumerate the ways they can meet. The third test is the one that punishes `<` instead of `<=`: they touch at hour 5, and touching counts because both ends are occupied.

exam.prompt: `same_price(a, b)` should report `True` when two amounts of money differ by less than 0.01, and `False` otherwise. It reports `False` for two amounts that a shopper would call identical. Repair it.
exam.starterCode:
def same_price(a, b):
    return a == b
exam.solution:
def same_price(a, b):
    return abs(a - b) < 0.01
exam.explain: `0.1 + 0.2` is stored as 0.30000000000000004, so exact equality is `False` even though the two amounts are the same money. Comparing the size of the gap against a tolerance is the standard repair; `abs` gives the gap without caring which amount was larger, and comparing `a - b < 0.01` alone would call 5.00 and 100.00 the same price.

exam.prompt: A shop's stock count is `0` when the shelf is empty and `None` when nobody has counted it yet. Explain why `if count:` cannot tell those two situations apart, and say what to write instead. Name both values in your answer.
exam.explain: Both values are falsy, so `if count:` sends both down the same branch and no error is raised - which is what makes it dangerous rather than merely wrong. The repair is to test for the meaning you have in mind: `count is None` for never counted, `count == 0` for sold out, in that order.
